description: Current browseable school/program set. Inclusion must be supported by at least one current school-fit field. Related fields—including marine biology, ecology, conservation biology, cognition, wildlife health, rehabilitation, and anthrozoology—may add context but do not independently qualify a program for this library.

programs.whyExplore: A broad animal-centered science degree that keeps zoology and organismal biology visible while leaving room for behavior and other specialties.
programs.lookFirst: Advanced zoology, physiology, behavior, and organismal electives; undergraduate research; how much ecology to include versus animal-focused science.

programs.whyExplore: A direct wildlife-biology route for understanding free-ranging animals, populations, field methods, and wildlife science.
programs.lookFirst: Wildlife field methods, vertebrate-focused courses, population biology, animal handling or tracking opportunities, and the balance of animals versus habitat/GIS work.

programs.whyExplore: A flexible biological-science route that can be shaped toward organismal biology and behavior without committing to an agricultural animal-science curriculum.
programs.lookFirst: Actual availability of animal physiology, behavior, zoology, and organismal electives; faculty research that uses animals; hands-on experience outside the major.

programs.whyExplore: A wildlife-focused concentration inside a large research university, useful when free-ranging wildlife remains a serious direction.
programs.lookFirst: How much of the concentration is animal/population biology versus habitat, policy, and spatial analysis; field research and wildlife-specific faculty projects.

programs.whyExplore: A four-year accredited veterinary-technology route combining clinical nursing, physiology, welfare, and advanced technical training, with exotics/behavior options.
programs.lookFirst: The required Amherst-to-Newton move after year two; clinical sequence; animal-welfare and exotics/behavior electives; senior internship settings.

programs.whyExplore: A dedicated animal-behavior degree where biology and psychology are integrated rather than behavior being only a small elective cluster.
programs.lookFirst: Behavior faculty and research, welfare-related coursework, internships, and how to add sustained hands-on husbandry or managed-animal experience if desired.

programs.whyExplore: The Animal Science option becomes much more relevant when paired with URI's Zoo and Aquarium Science certificate, adding zoo management and welfare to a managed-animal foundation.
programs.lookFirst: How much livestock/agricultural coursework is required; certificate scheduling; Zoo Animal Management and Zoo/Aquarium Animal Welfare; zoo-based and internship experience.

programs.whyExplore: A direct wildlife-biology pathway for field and population work when free-ranging animals are more appealing than managed-animal care.
programs.lookFirst: Wildlife courses and field experiences, animal versus habitat emphasis, quantitative requirements, and whether zoo/managed-animal interests would need the separate certificate.

programs.whyExplore: A useful hybrid for keeping wildlife biology while adding structured zoo/aquarium management and welfare coursework.
programs.lookFirst: Whether the combined major/certificate schedule is realistic; zoo-course prerequisites; direct animal experience; how the field-wildlife and managed-animal pieces fit together.

programs.whyExplore: Animal behavior and welfare are central, and the Zoo Biology minor adds a defined husbandry, enrichment, management, and zoo/aquarium internship pathway.
programs.lookFirst: Zoo Biology minor course rotation; Zoo Animal Management, husbandry, welfare, enrichment, observational methods, and internship sequencing.

programs.whyExplore: A rigorous Zoology B.S. with strong animal biology, behavior/physiology options, and undergraduate field or laboratory research.
programs.lookFirst: Behavior and physiology electives, faculty research, independent-study opportunities, and how much direct husbandry/animal-care experience would need to come from outside the curriculum.

programs.whyExplore: One of the most direct zoo-science undergraduate routes, with first-year animal work and a curriculum spanning husbandry, behavior, training, nutrition, health, exhibits, and zoo management.
programs.lookFirst: Required animal work and Experience360 internships; behavior/training/enrichment courses; zoo-management sequence; how specialized the degree feels compared with broader zoology.

programs.whyExplore: A Maine-based veterinary-technology program offering both associate and bachelor's degrees with extensive hands-on technical and laboratory training.
programs.lookFirst: Associate-versus-bachelor sequence, credentialing milestones, current clinical facilities, and opportunities to gain exotic/zoo/wildlife experience.

programs.whyExplore: A four-year veterinary-technology route that builds on SUNY Canton's long-established accredited associate curriculum and includes work with companion, farm, and laboratory animals.
programs.lookFirst: How A.A.S. requirements fit inside the B.S.; preceptorships; species mix; advanced bachelor's coursework; options relevant to zoo/wildlife or research settings.

programs.whyExplore: An unusually hands-on veterinary-technology path with live-animal labs from the first semester, an accredited A.A.S., and a B.S. continuation for advanced clinical, laboratory-animal, or public-health study.
programs.lookFirst: The A.A.S.-to-B.S. admission structure; live-animal labs; clinical facilities; advanced focus choices; how much zoo/exotic exposure would require external experience.
